questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: An essay built around a question
questions.learningObjective: Identify how a question organises an essay
questions.stem: In the file note recommending consent for a memorial panel, the planner argues that the text should be organised around a single question.

options.text: The argument holds, because a question gives the panel a shape and lets the answers arrive in order
The argument fails, because a longer statement persuades a committee more than a shorter one
options.misconception: believes length of document increases its persuasive force

options.text: The argument fails, because interpretive panels are only permitted to state dates, names and events
options.misconception: believes heritage panels are restricted to factual lists

options.text: The argument holds, because panels respond better to questions than to statements of historical fact
options.misconception: believes the panel's preference decides the argument's merit

questions.explanation: A question gives the text an ordering principle and lets the discussion build towards an answer. The panel's preference is beside the point.
questions.hint: Ask what the question does for the writing.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Three answers weighed as an argument
questions.learningObjective: Analyse how three answers can be weighed against evidence
questions.stem: A heritage statement weighs three explanations for the vacant yard and asks the panel to choose between them.

answer.exemplar: Weighing three answers means each one is stated in its strongest form, put against the evidence the file can actually supply, and then ranked by that evidence rather than by the writer's preference. The structure keeps the alternatives visible instead of smuggling the preferred one in under cover of a single narrative.

questions.explanation: Weighing means stating each answer fully and ranking them by the evidence the file supplies. The structure keeps alternatives visible, which a single confident narrative would have hidden.
questions.hint: Ask what the ranking is based on.

options.text: The memoir differs, because it was published by a private press and the autobiography by a council
options.misconception: judges the works by their publishers rather than their aims

options.text: The memoir differs, because it is written from remembered experience rather than from an institutional account
The memoir differs, because it was published after the town was consolidated into a single borough
options.misconception: treats administrative change as the source of the.

options.text: The memoir differs, because the autobiography was written to record events and the memoir to record places
options.misconception: reduces the difference to subject matter alone

questions.explanation: The memoir is organised around remembered experience, including what the writer felt and did, while the civic autobiography serves the institution's account of itself.

questions.learningObjective: Identify which of two books is a memoir

stimulus.body: A consultee's objection attaches two books. One was published in 1961 and recounts the writer's years as a market porter. The other was printed by the borough in 1904 to mark its centenary and covers the same district from 1800 to 1900.

questions.stem: The consultee's objection attaches two books, and the officer notes that only one of them is a memoir.

options.text: The 1904 volume is the memoir, because the porter's years were the borough's own and therefore public history
options.misconception: conflates personal experience with the institution's need.

options.text: The 1961 book is the memoir, because memoirs are always published later than the histories they sit beside
options.misconception: judges the form by publication date rather than by shape

options.text: The 1961 book is the memoir, because it is organised around a life remembered rather than a century surveyed
Neither is a memoir, because a memoir must cover a public life rather than an ordinary working one
options.misconception: assumes memoirs are reserved for public figures

questions.explanation: The 1961 book is organised around a life remembered, which is what makes it a memoir, while the centenary volume surveys a century for an institution.
questions.hint: Ask what each book is organised around.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A travelogue's method of looking
questions.learningObjective: Describe how a travelogue's method shapes what it records
questions.stem: Circulated with the application is a 1911 travelogue, and the planner asks how its author actually looked at the harbour.

answer.exemplar: The author looks the way a trained eye looks, and the method shows in the selection: she measures the harbour against the ships she has known, notes what the tide leaves behind, and passes over the housing because her genre did not treat it as scenery. A travelogue records a way of seeing as much as a place.

questions.explanation: A travelogue records a way of seeing, and its habits of attention decide what is worth reporting. Treating the omissions as simple gaps mistakes the method at work for an incomplete record.
questions.hint: Ask what the writer was trained to notice.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: An essay built around a question
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a question contributes to an essay's structure
questions.stem: Memo to the committee, the planner observes that the essay's opening question is doing the work of an argument.

answer.exemplar: The question does the work of an argument because it commits the essay to a testable claim and gathers its evidence around that test. A statement of fact only reports; a question sets a condition to be met, so the reader can tell in advance what the writer intends to show and can check whether it was shown.

questions.explanation: A question commits the essay to a testable claim and organises the evidence around it, which is why it can do an argument's work. Treating it as decoration ignores the commitment it makes visible.
questions.hint: Ask what the reader can check afterwards.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: A travelogue's method of looking
questions.learningObjective: Identify the method behind a travelogue's observations
questions.stem: The site visit notes describe a walk through the quarter, and the officer asks what method the walking employs.

answer.exemplar: The method is a route, and a route is a decision: the writer chose to arrive on foot, at walking pace, along the edges of the quarter rather than through its middle. That choice determines the sequence of impressions, what falls into view, and what the quarter appears to be, which is why two honest travellers can describe different places.

questions.explanation: A travelogue's method is its chosen route and pace, and that choice determines both the sequence of impressions and what counts as worth reporting.
questions.hint: Ask what path the writer chose to take.

options.misconception: assumes panels punish visible uncertainty

questions.explanation: A question the panel must test cannot be answered by assertion, which is precisely why it functions as a test rather than a conclusion. Visible uncertainty is a recognised method.

answer.exemplar: The attention was achieved by returning to the gatepost at different times, from different positions, and at different hours, so that what looked like one object became a record of how the street was entered and used. questions.topic: Memoir against autobiography
questions.learningObjective: Distinguish a memoir from an institutional account of a town
questions.stem: The correspondence file holds two documents, and the planner asks which one is a memoir rather than an official history.

answer.exemplar: The memoir remembers from inside a life and admits what the writer felt, misremembered and left out, while the official history assembles a sequence for the institution's benefit and leaves the writer's own part unremarked. options.text: Neither, because both versions are identical and so the question is not in dispute
options.misconception: misses that the difference lies in what follows the question

options.text: The second, because the pages that follow answer the question and so leave nothing to test

questions.explanation: The second version answers its own question with descriptive pages and so removes the test, while the first sets up evidence that can bear on it.
questions.hint: Ask what follows each version.

questions.topic: Sustained attention to a small site
questions.learningObjective: Explain what long attention to a small place reveals
questions.stem: In the site note, the planner explains what long attention to one doorway revealed about the whole terrace.

options.text: It revealed that the doorway was widened twice, which shows the terrace adapted rather than declined
It revealed nothing, because intimacy in theatre has never depended on where the audience is seated
options.misconception: historicises intimacy as a period fashion

options.text: It revealed that the doorway was modern, so the rest of the terrace is likely to be modern too
options.misconception: generalises from one feature to the whole terrace without.

options.text: It revealed that the doorway was widened twice, which proves the terrace was rebuilt to a uniform standard
options.misconception: reads a record of change as evidence of uniformity

questions.explanation: Two widenings show adaptation in response to use, which is a substantive reading of the terrace's history. Scarcity and a modern repair do not stop a detail supporting an inference.
questions.hint: Ask what each change in the opening records.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: An essay built around a question
questions.learningObjective: Treat a question as a working tool in an essay
questions.stem: The committee's question is written into the report's opening, and the planner treats it as a working tool.

options.text: Treating it as a tool is right, because a committee question always improves the quality of an appraisal
options.misconception: assumes questions from committees are automatically good.

options.text: Treating it as a tool is right, because it directs where evidence is gathered and what a finding counts as
Treating it as a tool is wrong, because the officer's own method should decide what the report examines
options.misconception: believes the writer's method must displace the question

options.text: Treating it as a tool is wrong, because a question commits the report to a conclusion it should not reach
options.misconception: believes a framing question predetermines the outcome

questions.explanation: A working question directs the gathering of evidence and defines what counts as a finding, which is why the planner can treat it as a tool. Committee questions are not automatically good.
questions.hint: Ask what the question organises in the writing.

options.misconception: treats the order of composition as evidence of strength

options.text: Because it is the longest, and length of treatment shows the writer had most to say about it
options.misconception: treats length of treatment as evidence of strength

Because it is the most recent account, and recent accounts correct the errors of older ones

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Memoir against autobiography
questions.learningObjective: Identify a memoir and an official history in one file
questions.stem: Memo to the chair, the planner sets out a memoir and a civic history side by side and says which is which.

answer.exemplar: The memoir is the work of the woman who worked the weaving shed and who had to answer for a life she partly disliked, while the civic history was written for the borough's anniversary and had to leave the shed in a decent light. Set beside each other they show how the same stretch of years is described from inside a life and from outside an institution.

questions.explanation: The memoir writer is answerable for a life, the civic writer for the institution's anniversary, and the contrast shows how the same years look from each position.
questions.hint: Ask who each writer had to please.

questions.subject: ENGLISH_LITERATURE
questions.topic: Two books, one memoir
questions.learningObjective: Weigh two books and justify marking the memoir
questions.stem: In the concluding note, the planner weighs the two books in the file and says why only one of them is a memoir.

options.text: The typescript is the memoir, because memoirs are always shorter than the histories they sit beside
options.misconception: judges the genre by the length of the book

options.text: The typescript is the memoir, because it was written later and so has had longer to settle
options.misconception: treats later writing as more reliable by default

options.text: The printed history is the memoir, because it was written by the people the book describes
options.misconception: confuses authorship by the subject with self-narration

options.text: The typescript is the memoir, because it answers for a remembered life rather than for the borough

questions.explanation: The synthesis ties the genre distinction to its evidentiary use, which is what the note needs to say. A version that only labels the two books leaves the panel without knowing what to do with them.
questions.hint: Ask what each book can testify to.
